Photograph: James Ross/AAP Queensland Alleged rapist arrested after returning to Brisbane crime scene that night, police say Man, 32, charged with six counts of rape, stalking and assault after woman was allegedly attacked in Brookfield Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Ben Smee Thu 20 Aug 2026 23.14 EDT Last modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 23.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Queensland police say a man accused of raping and assaulting a young woman, who was taking a morning bushwalk, has been arrested after he returned to the crime scene in his vehicle later that evening. A woman, aged in her 20s, was walking in the semi-rural Brisbane suburb of Brookfield about 6.30am on Thursday when she was allegedly stopped by the man and sexually assaulted. She told police her attacker fled on foot. Later that afternoon, police arrested a 32-year-old man from Raceview, near Ipswich, nearby. Det Supt Andrew Massingham told reporters the attack had been random and that the alleged attacker had been on his way to work. “We will then allege that when he completed work that day, he drove back past the crime scene,” Massingham said on Friday. Massingham said that after an urgent public appeal for information on Thursday, two people came forward with dashcam footage that was “the final piece of the puzzle”. “Officers identified the vehicle as being similar,” Massingham said. “They followed the vehicle, and he was actually intercepted.” The man has been charged with six counts of rape, stalking, assault with intent to commit rape, assault causing bodily harm and deprivation of liberty. Police said they will allege the man had approached the woman from behind near the Brookfield Road bridge. Police said the woman was now being cared for by family. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Massingham said he wanted to “acknowledge her bravery in coming forward”. “The [alleged victim] is at home with her family. Prefer Newsweek on Google to see more of our trusted coverage when you search. On August 16, a Spanish F-18 flying a NATO air policing mission shot down a drone that had entered Romanian airspace. Four days later, two Romanian F-16s were scrambled after a maritime drone was detected near the Neptun Alpha offshore platform, part of the Neptun Deep natural gas project and a critical asset for Europe’s energy security. Neither incident resulted in loss of life. That is welcome news, but it should not give us false comfort. What happened in the Black Sea points to a security problem NATO can no longer afford to ignore: How do we act when an unidentified threat approaches allied territory, seconds matter, but attribution may take hours or days? Read More on Opinion This is the reality of gray-zone warfare. An adversary no longer needs to launch a conventional, full-scale attack to create disruption. A cheap drone that tests reaction times, approaches an energy installation or creates uncertainty about its origin and intent can already serve a strategic purpose. Making decision-makers hesitate is often the real aim. ... That escalation is not theoretical. On September 13, a drone struck the locomotive of a passenger train traveling from Kyiv to Warsaw, just kilometers from the Polish border, minutes after a separate train carrying senior European officials, including former prime ministers of the United Kingdom and Sweden, had passed through the same area. No one was hurt. But the incident was not incidental: gray-zone tactics are reaching the transport corridors that connect Ukraine to NATO territory, and the people who depend on them, including senior European officials. As Romania’s deputy prime minister for strategic partnerships and minister of justice, I worked for years on national security and Black Sea issues, including as co-chair of the U.S.-Romania Strategic Partnership Dialogue in Bucharest. That experience reinforced one non-negotiable lesson: uncertainty must never become an excuse for inaction. NATO cannot afford to wait for definitive attribution before protecting its people. But speed must not mean improvisation. Commanders need pre-authorized rules based on a threat’s behavior, trajectory, proximity to protected assets and risk to civilians. The goal is to give commanders a lawful basis for proportionate and timely action when a threat presents an imminent risk, not to turn every unidentified object into a target. It is to make clear to any potential adversary that testing NATO’s airspace, critical infrastructure and decision-making will not produce hesitation or paralysis; that the alliance is prepared to act. That is deterrence. Asking pilots or field commanders to solve complex legal and political equations in midair is unfair and dangerous. A fighter pilot has seconds to react. An intelligence team may need hours or days to establish where a system came from and who launched it. Designing our air defenses on the assumption that these timelines will naturally align is a recipe for failure. This is as much a legal and political problem as an operational one. Under current peacetime arrangements, the authority to use force in defense of national airspace remains a national prerogative. We saw this in Poland, where the Polish Operational Commander decided to neutralize drones that posed a threat, with Polish and allied aircraft involved in the response. Because each member state relies on its own arrangements, the alliance is left with a patchwork of national protocols. As a former minister of justice, I know that military authorization is of little use if the decision-making process is slowed by fragmented responsibilities or bureaucratic sign-offs. NATO needs a fast-track operational protocol that defines, in advance, when and under what conditions commanders can engage a high-risk threat. When an unidentified object enters allied airspace or approaches critical infrastructure, the chain of command must be fast enough to match the threat. The authority to act must be established long before a crisis begins, not negotiated on a secure line while a drone is heading toward a populated area or an offshore energy platform. We also cannot ignore a blunt economic reality. Scrambling a multimillion-dollar fighter jet or launching a high-end interceptor to deal with a cheap, mass-produced drone cannot remain our default response. High-end systems are vital when lives or critical infrastructure are at serious risk. But NATO also needs a broader and more flexible tool kit. At the NATO Summit Defence Industry Forum in Ankara in July, Secretary-General Mark Rutte announced the NATO Drone Edge Initiative, under which allies will invest more than $40 billion in counter-drone capabilities over the next five years. This investment is significant. It now needs to be matched by a unified operational doctrine that translates these resources into clear rules of engagement. The capabilities are already there. NATO’s European members need to bring them together into a layered air-defense system, combining sensors, command and control, electronic warfare, low-cost interceptors and short-range systems. As technology matures, we must integrate directed-energy weapons into that tool kit. The alliance must match the tool to the threat. At the same time, we must develop the right tools to make countering these threats economically sustainable. For Romania and our Black Sea neighbors, this is not an academic debate. Strategic energy assets such as Neptun Deep are vital to Europe’s energy security and resilience. Protecting them must be part of baseline defensive planning. The same applies to ports, power plants, communications infrastructure and military facilities across the alliance. Romania has already demonstrated what practical cooperation can look like. In April, it hosted the first event in NATO’s LCI-X counter-UAS series at Capu Midia military training range. However, these exercises must do more than test equipment. They must test decision-making: Who has the authority to act? How quickly can that authority be exercised? And what happens when the available intelligence is incomplete? But deterrence depends on more than military capabilities. Allies also need shared situational awareness, a clear political decision-making process and timely communication to commanders and the public. In a gray-zone environment, fragmented information or contradictory messages can create the very uncertainty an adversary seeks to exploit. NATO must therefore rehearse not only how it will intercept a threat, but how it will see the same threat, decide what to do about it and communicate that decision clearly. For those of us on NATO’s eastern flank, the gray zone is no longer an abstract concept. It is part of daily security. The alliance already has the technology, the capabilities and the experience to respond. What it needs now is the political courage to give commanders clear rules and the authority to act when time matters more than certainty. The next drone will not give us hours to debate. We must not waste those precious seconds figuring out what our rules are. Ana Birchall is a former deputy prime minister for Romania’s Strategic Partnerships, minister of justice and minister delegate for European affairs. A graduate of Yale Law School, she works with Champions Speakers Agency as an international politics and geopolitics speaker. The views expressed in this article are the writer's own. The Witcher is a fantasy franchise which is currently experiencing a massive heyday, with a fifth and final season of the Netflix show slated for release sometime in 2027, alongside a new expansion for the universally beloved, 11-year-old video game The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt from CD Projekt Red and the start of their next saga, The Witcher 4 , following in 2028. But now we've gotten the extremely exciting announcement that Andrzej Sapkowski , the author who started it all, is returning to his dark fantasy world for another book. Even better, he's already got a clear idea of when he should be done writing it â which means we have a rough idea of when it could release. This news comes from The Witcher fan page WiedÅºminlandia (via Redanian Intelligence ), who had boots on the ground at Copernicon in Torun, Poland this weekend, where Sapkowski was part of the programming. During an on-stage chat about his work, the author revealed that he hopes to finish work on the next Witcher novel by the end of 2027. Sapkowski didn't confirm any other details about the book, but he did reject a question from one fan about the possibility of future Witcher stories being centered around characters other than Geralt, such as Yennefer of Vengerberg . As such, it seems safe to assume this will be another adventure with Geralt of Rivia at the heart of it. Crossroads of Ravens by Andrzej Sapkowski (The Witcher) | Image courtesy of Orbit When will Andrzej Sapkowski's new Witcher book be published? The last book that Sapkowski published, Crossroads of Ravens , was released in Poland in late 2024, before seeing a worldwide release on September 30, 2025. Redanian Intelligence speculates we could see a similar timetable for this new Witcher book as well, and I'm inclined to agree. If Sapkowski hits his goal of completing it by the end of 2027, then it will probably launch in Poland sometime in 2028, then in the rest of the world in 2029. While that may sound like it's quite a while from now, this is actually an encouragingly fast turnaround for a brand new book in The Witcher series. It would mark the shortest time between books since the fourth and fifth novels of the main saga, Tower of Swallows and The Lady of the Lake , which were published in Poland two years apart in 1997 and 1999. After that, it seemed like Sapkowski was finished with Geralt, until he returned for the "sidequel" novel Season of Storms in 2013, which was a standalone tale that takes place around the same time as the short story collections The Last Wish and Sword of Destiny . Then there was another 11 year gap before the author's next work, Crossroads of Ravens , published in 2024. The fact that a tentative 4 years might pass between Crossroads of Ravens and this new book indicates Sapkowski is gaining steam. It's rare to see an author return to a series they had presumably finished years later and suddenly start churning out new books, but that seems to be the position Witcher fans are finding themselves in. It's a good place to be! Andrzej Sapkowski's The Witcher: The Last WishâThe Complete Collection. | Image: Dark Horse Books. What will Andrzej Sapkowski's new Witcher book be about? Another big question is of course what this novel will be about. Crossroads of Ravens was a prequel, and technically the earliest story Sapkowski has told about Geralt's life on the Path. It followed some of the witcher's very first adventures after he leaves Kaer Morhen, when he's only 18 years old and still trying to find his way in the world. Despite being a discreet adventure, it read more like a culmination of all the work Sapkowski had put into the saga so far; in my opinion, it's one of the most all-around solid books in the entire series . All we know about the new Witcher book right now is that it will probably be about Geralt. But will it be a continuation of Crossroads of Ravens , bridging the gap from the end of that book to the short stories in The Last Wish , where the witcher meets his long-term companions Dandelion and Yennefer of Vengerberg? Will it jump to a different period of Geralt's life, similar to Season of Storms ? Either seems possible until we hear more from Sapkowski. For now, it's just exciting to know that the author is feeling invigorated enough to keep writing new tales for Geralt of Rivia and his friends. And on the bright side, we'll have plenty to keep us busy until the book arrives, between The Witcher season 5, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt â Songs of the Past , and The Witcher 4 . The next Witcher book release on the calendar is Andrzej Sapkowski's The Witcher: The Last WishâThe Complete Collection , a deluxe graphic novel release of the short stories in The Last Wish from Dark Horse Books. It's out on December 15, 2026, wherever books are sold. Add us as a preferred source on Google Follow Loading recommendations...
